Ricarda Lang: German politician (born 1994). Ricarda Lang (born 17 January 1994) is a German politician of the Alliance 90/The Greens who has been serving as a member of the Bundestag since 2021.
Produced annually by WWE since 1988, this event's signature match sees wrestlers enter the ring one at a time on a timer rather than all at once — what's the event?
Royal Rumble: World Wrestling Entertainment event series.
This French explorer crossed the Atlantic some two dozen times, drew the first accurate maps of North America's eastern coast and Great Lakes, and founded Quebec City in 1608. Who was he?
Samuel de Champlain: French explorer of North America (1574–1635)
Born in Leptis Magna in Roman Africa, this general emerged as the final victor of the chaotic Year of the Five Emperors to rule Rome from 193 to 211 — who is he?
Septimius Severus: Roman emperor from 193 to 211. Lucius Septimius Severus (Latin: [ˈluːkius sepˈtimius seˈweːrus]; 11 April 145 – 4 February 211) was Roman emperor from 193 to 211.
Fought in two stages, a winter and summer campaign from 1614 to 1615, this conflict ended the Toyotomi clan and cemented Tokugawa rule over Japan — which historic clash?
Siege of Osaka: 1614-15 series of battles in Japan at the end of the Sengoku Period.
Dubbed the "King of Gambling," this billionaire held a 40-year government monopoly over Macau's casinos and split his fortune among children who run MGM Macau and City of Dreams — who was he?

Fought from 1992 to 1997, this Central Asian conflict pitted rebels from the Garm and Gorno-Badakhshan regions, organized as the United Tajik Opposition, against a Russian-backed government — which conflict was it?
Tajikistani Civil War: Armed conflict in Tajikistan from 1992 to 1997.
Chief minister who engineered Henry VIII's break from Rome to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, this powerful statesman was beheaded in 1540 — a loss the king later regretted. Who was he?
The son of a shipping magnate who founded OOCL, this businessman became Hong Kong's very first Chief Executive when sovereignty transferred in 1997 — who was he?
Tung Chee-hwa: Politician and businessman from Hong Kong.
Serving as the 18th U.S. ambassador to NATO before rising to Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, this diplomat briefly served as acting deputy secretary of state in 2023 — who is she?
Erupting in 1793 as a peasant revolt that turned Royalist, this French Revolutionary-era conflict was fought south of the Loire river and gave its combatants the nickname "Vendeans" — what was it?
War in the Vendée: 1793–1796 set of battles between the French revolutionaries and the royalists.
First built in the 11th century after the Norman conquest, this Berkshire royal residence has been used by the monarch since Henry I, making it the longest-occupied palace in Europe — which is it?
Windsor Castle: Official country residence of British monarch.
Made by young Indonesians on 28 October 1928, this nationalist declaration proclaimed one motherland, one nation, and one unifying language — what is it called?
Youth Pledge: 1928 declaration by Indonesian nationalists.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four. Thomas Carlyle (4 December 1795 – 5 February 1881) was a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
Which of these four began earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
John Cockcroft is a physicist. Ernest Rutherford accepted Cockcroft as a research student in the Cavendish Laboratory, and Cockcroft completed his doctorate under Rutherford's supervision in 1928.
Who among these is a chemist?
Linus Pauling is a chemist. Linus Carl Pauling ( PAW-ling; February 28, 1901 – August 19, 1994) was an American chemist and peace activist.
What is the atomic number of Nobelium?
Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol No and atomic number 102.
In what year was Katherine Johnson born?
Katherine Johnson: The space agency noted her "historical role as one of the first African-American women to work as a NASA scientist".
In what year was Ratan Tata born?
Ratan Tata: Ratan Naval Tata (28 December 1937 – 9 October 2024) was an Indian industrialist and philanthropist.
In what year was Ursula von der Leyen born?
Ursula von der Leyen: Von der Leyen was born and raised in Brussels, Belgium, to German parents.
In what year did Jean Piaget die?
Jean Piaget: Jean William Fritz Piaget (9 August 1896 – 16 September 1980) was a Swiss psychologist known for his work on child development.
In what year did Doc Holliday die?
Doc Holliday: Holliday is best known for his role in the events surrounding and his participation in the gunfight at the O.K.
In what year was Radon discovered?
Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.
In what year was Adenosine triphosphate discovered?
Adenosine triphosphate: When consumed in a metabolic process, ATP converts either to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) or to adenosine monophosphate (AMP).
Mil Mi-26: Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. The Mil Mi-26 (Russian: Миль Ми-26, NATO reporting name: Halo) is a Soviet/Russian heavy transport helicopter.
Which country is Artemy Lebedev from?
Artemy Lebedev: Russia. Artemy Andreyevich Lebedev (Russian: Артемий Андреевич Лебедев; born 13 February 1975) is a Russian designer, entrepreneur and Internet personality.
Who is credited with discovering Rhodium?
Rhodium: William Hyde Wollaston. Rhodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rh and atomic number 45.
Who is credited with discovering Ibuprofen?
Ibuprofen: Stewart Adams. Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation.
Who is credited with discovering Carbon?
Carbon: Antoine Lavoisier. Carbon (from Latin carbo 'coal') is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
Drugs that meddle with this neurotransmitter can do everything from paralyze to cause convulsions, since it's the signal motor neurons use to activate muscles. What is it?
Acetylcholine (ACh) is an organic compound that functions in the brain and body of many types of animals (including humans) as a neurotransmitter.
This genus of more than 650 flowering succulent species includes a 'true' member cultivated worldwide as the standard source for a soothing pharmaceutical gel — what's the genus?
Aloe (also written Alo) is a genus containing over 650 species of flowering succulent plants.
Nicknamed 'the heart of the scorpion,' this distinctly reddish variable star is the brightest in the constellation Scorpius — what is it?
Antares is the brightest star in the constellation of Scorpius. It has the Bayer designation α Scorpii, which is Latinised to Alpha Scorpii.
A methyl ester built from aspartic acid and phenylalanine, this non-saccharide sweetener is among the most-studied food additives ever, judged safe by over 100 regulatory bodies — what is it?
Aspartame is an artificial, non-saccharide sweetener commonly used as a sugar substitute in foods and beverages.
Their foliage is almost indistinguishable from a cycad's, but flower-like reproductive organs — some likely insect-pollinated — set these common Mesozoic seed plants apart. Which extinct order?
Bennettitales (also known as cycadeoids) is an extinct order of seed plants that first appeared in the Permian period and became extinct in most areas toward the end of the Cretaceous.
Native to the Mediterranean and also called 'starflower,' this annual herb's seeds are pressed for oil even though the plant carries mild toxic alkaloids — which plant?
Borage (or; Borago officinalis), also known as starflower, is an annual herb in the flowering plant family Boraginaceae native to the Mediterranean region.
Its three-dimensional shape mimics adenosine closely enough to plug into the same receptors, blocking the brain's signal to wind down — which psychoactive substance is it?
Caffeine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant of the methylxanthine class and is the most commonly consumed psychoactive substance globally.
Mature females are cows, the intact males are bulls, and the castrated males pull plows as oxen — all names for one widespread domesticated bovine kept as livestock. What animal is it?
Cattle (Bos taurus) are large, domesticated, bovid ungulates widely kept as livestock.
Grown for blue-flowered roadside roots that become a coffee substitute, or for bitter salad leaves like escarole and radicchio, which plant genus covers both chicory and endive?
Cichorium is a genus of plants in the tribe Cichorieae within the family Asteraceae.

Often called the most renowned Greek mathematician since antiquity, he spent his career in Germany advancing measure theory and the calculus of variations — and even built an axiomatic formulation of thermodynamics. Who was he?
Constantin Carathéodory (13 September 1873 - 2 February 1950) was a Greek mathematician who spent most of his professional career in Germany.
As of December 2025 worth an estimated $8.7 billion, this Swedish businessman founded and chairs a massive music-streaming company — who is he?
Daniel Ek (Swedish; born 21 February 1983) is a Swedish businessman and technologist.

England-born but raised in Australia, this geologist did much of his real rock-hunting in the Flinders Ranges — though he's better remembered for braving the ice alongside Shackleton on the Nimrod Expedition; who was he?
Douglas Mawson (5 May 1882 - 14 October 1958) was an Australian geologist, Antarctic explorer, and academic.
Psychology, medicine, history, and even computer science all study these pleasure-or-displeasure states, which still lack any agreed scientific definition — what are they?
Emotion are physical and mental states brought on by neurophysiological changes, variously associated with thoughts, feelings, behavioral responses, and a degree of pleasure or displeasure.
This sensory organ detects light and converts it into electro-chemical signals in neurons, using an adjustable lens system to focus incoming light and form images — name the organ?
Eye is a sensory organ that allows an organism to perceive visual information.
Sitting just below caesium as the second-most electropositive element, this alkali metal decays so fast that a bulk sample has never actually been seen — what is it?
Francium is a chemical element; it has symbol Fr and atomic number 87.
Before he founded a piece of the U.S. aircraft industry, this pioneer set an unofficial world speed record astride a V8-powered motorcycle that stood unbroken until 1911. Who was he?
Glenn Curtiss (May 21, 1878 - July 23, 1930) was an American aviation and motorcycling pioneer, and a founder of the U.S.
Named for a flattened, laterally extended head shape called a cephalofoil, with eyes placed at each end of the T, this family of sharks includes species mostly grouped in one genus — which sharks?

Hammerhead shark are a group of sharks that form the family Sphyrnidae, named for the unusual and distinctive form of their heads, which are flattened and laterally extended into a cephalofoil (a T-shape or "hammer").
This perennial root vegetable, a relative of mustard, wasabi, broccoli, and cabbage, is grated and used worldwide as a pungent spice and condiment — what plant is it?
Representing about three-quarters of circulating antibodies in humans, which type of antibody is released by plasma B cells?
Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is a type of antibody.
An economist-turned-pundit who rose to fame on Argentine TV talk shows, who became the nation's 57th president in 2023 under the banner La Libertad Avanza?
Javier Milei (born 22 October 1970) is an Argentine politician and economist who has served as the 57th president of Argentina since 2023.
This anesthetic drug induces a trance-like dissociative state while preserving breathing, and its S-enantiomer is now used to treat depression — name it?
Ketamine is a cyclohexanone-derived general anesthetic and NMDA receptor antagonist with analgesic and hallucinogenic properties, used medically for anesthesia, depression, and pain management.
Its pale golden coat is patterned not with simple dots but with dark spots clustered into rings called rosettes, and it has prowled Africa and Asia since the Early Pleistocene — which big cat is it?
Leopard (Panthera pardus) is one of the five extant cat species in the genus Panthera.
Named for their strong, monogamous pair bonding and the long stretches paired birds spend sitting together, this small genus of African parrots is popular as a pet — what is it commonly called?
Lovebird is the common name for the genus Agapornis, a small group of parrots in the Old World parrot family Psittaculidae.
Cold-sensitive and tasting of sweet pine and citrus, this kitchen herb is so close to its cousin that in parts of the Middle East the two names are used interchangeably with oregano. What is it?
This branch of economics studies how individuals and firms allocate scarce resources within individual markets, as opposed to the economy as a whole — what field is it?

Microeconomics is a branch of economics that studies the behavior of individuals and firms in making decisions regarding the allocation of scarce resources and the interactions among these individuals and firms.
Scholars can't even agree on which elements define it, yet it appears in every human society as a vehicle for creativity through composition and performance — what is it?
Music is the arrangement of sound to create some combination of form, harmony, melody, rhythm, or otherwise expressive content.
This raised region of tissue on the breast, surrounded by the darker-colored areola, is where milk exits the body through the lactiferous ducts during breastfeeding — name this body part?
Nipple is a raised region of tissue on the surface of the breast from which, in lactating females, milk from the mammary gland leaves the body through the lactiferous ducts to nurse an infant.
Found on every continent except Antarctica, this fish-eating raptor nests near water and can be identified by its brown back and pale, grayish head — what bird is it?
Osprey (Pandion haliaetus), historically known as sea hawk, river hawk, and fish hawk, is a diurnal, fish-eating bird of prey with a cosmopolitan range.
About 3,000 varieties of this apple-like fruit exist worldwide, and its fermented juice is known as perry — which fruit is it?
Pear are a genus of trees, Pyrus, in the family Rosaceae, that bear an edible apple-like fruit of the same name.
Native to Chile and Peru and cultivated since Inca times, this nightshade fruit is known in English as the Cape gooseberry or goldenberry — what is its scientific name?
Physalis peruviana is a species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) native to Chile and Peru.
Element number 19, this silvery alkali metal reacts so eagerly with air that it forms flaky white peroxide within seconds — and its symbol K comes from the Neo-Latin word kalium. What is it?
Potassium is a chemical element; it has symbol K (from Neo-Latin kalium) and atomic number 19.
Its blossoms are a beloved symbol of early spring throughout East Asia, and its crunchy fruit is marketed globally as the Asian or nashi pear - which tree species?
Pyrus pyrifolia is a species of pear tree native to southern China and northern Indochina that has been introduced to Korea, Japan and other parts of the world.

An emeritus fellow of an Oxford college and the first-ever holder of a professorship for the public understanding of science, this British evolutionary biologist is also known as a prominent atheist author — who is he?
Richard Dawkins (born 26 March 1941) is a British evolutionary biologist, zoologist, science communicator, noted atheist, and author.
Having coded his first game in high school and studied computer science in Tokyo, this man went on to lead Nintendo by championing fun over raw horsepower — who is he?
Satoru Iwata (December 6, 1959 - July 11, 2015) was a Japanese businessman, video game programmer and producer.
Despite its long-nosed, mouse-like look, this small mammal is actually a closer cousin to hedgehogs and moles than to rodents — what is it?
Shrew (family Soricidae) are small mole-like mammals classified in the order Eulipotyphla.

This class of moisture-loving hexapods — the largest lineage of six-legged creatures excluded from the insect group — indirectly aids decomposition by breaking down organic matter and shaping soil microbial life. What are they?
Springtail (class Collembola) form the largest of the three lineages of modern hexapods that are no longer considered insects, the others being Protura and Diplura.
Down, Wolf–Hirschhorn, and Andersen–Tawil are all named examples of this medical term for a cluster of correlated signs and symptoms — what is it?
Syndrome is a set of medical signs and symptoms which are correlated with each other and often associated with a particular disease or disorder.
This American economist and social theorist, a prominent voice in the conservative movement, received the National Humanities Medal from President George W. Bush in 2002 — who is he?
Thomas Sowell (SOHL; born June 30, 1930) is an American economist, economic historian, and social theorist.
Egypt and Iraq both flew this Soviet-designed jet bomber in wars against Israel, and China still produces an updated license-built version, the H-6K — which aircraft?
Tupolev Tu-16 (USAF/DOD reporting name Type 39; NATO reporting name: Badger) is a twin-engined jet strategic heavy bomber used by the Soviet Union.
This canid genus contains the 'true foxes' — smaller and bushier-tailed than any wolf or jackal, typically living two to four years, occasionally a decade — which genus?
Vulpes is a genus of the subfamily Caninae.

This Polish-American scholar served as Jimmy Carter's national security advisor from 1977 to 1981 and helped organize an influential international policy group known as the Trilateral Commission — who is he?
Zbigniew Brzezinski (March 28, 1928 - May 26, 2017) was a Polish-American diplomat and political scientist.
This term for cancer that begins in gland cells applies to the most common form of breast cancer and one of the two major types of esophageal cancer — which term?
De Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter
Adenocarcinoma: Cancer of epithelial cells with glandular origin or characteristics.

Often called the greatest mathematician of the twentieth century, this German-born Frenchman revolutionized algebraic geometry before abruptly leaving his post at a Paris research institute in 1970 — who is he?

These coiled-shelled cephalopods, more closely related to octopuses than to nautiluses despite the resemblance, thrived from the Devonian until vanishing around the dinosaur extinction 66 million years ago — what are they?
Ammonoidea: Extinct subclass of cephalopod molluscs.
Useless against the cold, the flu, or any fungus, this kind of medicine works only by killing or stalling bacteria — what is it called?
Antibiotic: Antimicrobial substance active against bacteria.

This umbrella term for joint disease covers conditions like osteoarthritis, most common in weight-bearing joints as people age, and the autoimmune form that typically targets the hands and feet. What condition is this?
This Indian jurist studied economics at Columbia and the London School of Economics before becoming the chief architect of his country's constitution. Who was he?
B. R. Ambedkar: Indian jurist, economist, politician and social reformer (1891–1956)
One of the richest people alive, this French chairman and CEO turned his father's construction firm toward real estate before building the world's largest luxury-goods empire — who is he?
Credited with kicking off the Jet Age, this swept-wing quadjet airliner entered regular passenger service with Pan Am in October 1958 — which aircraft?

Best known for his role as Ben Hunter in a soapy prime-time revenge drama, this American actor also starred as Will Davis on The CW's 'Privileged' and Kyle Parks on Lifetime's 'The Client List.' Who is he?
Formed when quicklime reacts with water, this compound goes by names like slaked lime and builders' lime, and is used in food prep under the additive code E526 — what is it?
Calcium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Ca(OH)2.

This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' for reactions that work inside living systems, building chemical tools to study the cell-surface sugars called glycans. Who is she?
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like herb is brewed into calming teas and can trigger uterine contractions in its Roman variety — what is it?
Chamomile: Common name for several daisy-like plants.
In this chronic liver condition, healthy tissue is replaced by scar tissue and regenerative nodules, choking blood flow and causing portal hypertension — what is it called?
Cirrhosis: Chronic disease of the liver, characterized by fibrosis.

Nicknamed 'flying lemurs' despite not being lemurs at all, these Southeast Asian gliding mammals are primates' closest living relatives and belong to an order whose name means 'skin wing' — what are they called?
Its round nuts distinguish it from the longer filbert, and its coppiced wood once built wattle-and-daub walls across England — which shrub?
Corylus avellana: Species of tree (common hazel)
Two polynucleotide chains coil around each other into a double helix to carry the genetic instructions of nearly every living thing — what is this macromolecule?
DNA: Molecule that carries genetic information.
Sold under the brand name Valium, this benzodiazepine anxiolytic treats anxiety, seizures, alcohol withdrawal, and muscle spasms — and can even induce memory loss during procedures; what is it?
Diazepam: Benzodiazepine sedative. Diazepam, sold under the brand name Valium among others, is a medication of the benzodiazepine family that acts as an anxiolytic.
The only living relative of the extinct Steller's sea cow, this seagrass-grazing marine mammal is most abundant in the waters of northern Australia — what is it?
Dugong: Species of marine mammal. It is one of four living species of the order Sirenia, which also includes three species of manatees.
The first woman admitted to MIT, this environmental chemist was the first to apply chemistry to nutrition and founded the home economics movement — who was she?
Ellen Swallow Richards: American engineer and chemist (1843–1911)
The major female sex hormone, this estrogen drives the development of secondary sexual characteristics and helps maintain reproductive tissues from puberty through pregnancy — what is it?

Recognized by their pod-like fruit and compound leaves, this plant family — the third-largest among flowering plants — includes beans, peas, and lentils along with genera like Acacia and Mimosa. What family is it?
Fabaceae: Family of legume flowering plants. Fabaceae or Leguminosae, commonly known as the legume, pea, or bean family, is a large and agriculturally important family of flowering plants.
This whip-like appendage propels sperm cells and lets bacteria like Helicobacter pylori swim through stomach mucus, sometimes triggering ulcers — what is it called?
Flagellum: Cellular appendage functioning as locomotive or sensory organelle.

Unlike plants, this kingdom of life can't photosynthesize, and unlike most things, it has chitin in its cell walls — feeding instead by oozing digestive enzymes out and absorbing what dissolves. What group includes yeasts, molds, and mushrooms?
Fungus: Organism belonging to kingdom Fungi.

The largest species of its kind in the world, this circumglobal sea creature was reclassified in 2017 after DNA testing showed it was more closely related to a different genus than to its smaller reef-dwelling cousin — what is it?
Giant oceanic manta ray: Species of cartilaginous fish.
Known as the black shag in New Zealand, this widespread seabird breeds across much of the Old World, Australasia, and the Atlantic coast of North America — which bird?

Recognizable by V-shaped nostrils and a layer of blubber that keeps it warm in Arctic and temperate coastal waters, this pinniped is the most widely distributed of its kind and can weigh up to 370 pounds — which species?
Harbor seal: Species of pinniped. Blubber under the seal's skin helps to maintain body temperature.
This seasonal state of drastically reduced metabolism, breathing, and heart rate lets animals conserve energy through winter months, with 'aestivation' as its summer counterpart — what is it called?
Hibernation: Physiological state of dormant inactivity in order to pass the winter season.
This poisonous gas or liquid with the formula HF dissolves in water to form a corrosive acid and serves as the chief industrial source of fluorine — what is it?
Native to the subcontinent, the male of this bird species is called a peacock and sports a fan-shaped crest with a dazzling train of eyespot feathers used in courtship — which species?
Indian peafowl: Species of bird. The Indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus), also known as the common peafowl, or blue peafowl, is a species of peafowl native to the Indian subcontinent.
Awarded a gas-attack Iron Cross in WWI before sharing the 1925 Nobel with Gustav Hertz for the laws of how an electron strikes an atom — who was this German-American physicist?
This Hungarian-American polymath helped build the mathematical framework of quantum physics and codified ideas from game theory to cellular automata — who was he?
John von Neumann: Hungarian and American mathematician and physicist (1903–1957)
A biologist and botanist married four times — her last husband directed the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos lab — she was played by Emily Blunt in a 2023 film. Who was she?
Spread through the bite of sandflies, this parasitic disease can appear in cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral forms, the last marked by fever and an enlarged spleen — what is it called?
Leishmaniasis: Disease caused by parasites of the Leishmania type.

This catch-all name covers over 7,000 squamate species on every continent but Antarctica — from finger-length geckos to the three-meter Komodo dragon, with a few 'legless' lineages thrown in. What is it?
Found from Gibraltar to across Asia, these Old World monkeys live in troops centered on dominant matriarchs, and one Malaysian species eats about 70 rats a year — what are they?
Macaque: Genus of Old World monkeys. The macaques constitute a genus (Macaca) of gregarious Old World monkeys of the subfamily Cercopithecinae.
Kangaroos, koalas, and wombats all belong to this mammal group whose young are born undeveloped and finish developing in their mother's pouch — what group is it?
Marsupial: Infraclass of mammals in the clade Metatheria.
The only operational rocket-powered fighter ever fielded, this WWII German interceptor became the first piloted aircraft to exceed 1,000 km/h in level flight — which aircraft?

Messerschmitt Me 163 Komet: German rocket-powered interceptor. The Messerschmitt Me 163 Komet is a rocket-powered interceptor aircraft primarily designed and produced by the German aircraft manufacturer Messerschmitt.
Named for the Latin for 'thousand feet,' no species of this many-legged arthropod class was confirmed to have 1,000-plus legs until a 2020 discovery with over 1,300 — what are they?
Millipede: Class of arthropods. Its primary defence mechanism is to curl into a tight coil, thereby protecting its legs and other vital delicate areas on the body behind a hard exoskeleton.
Named for a Tanzanian teenager who studied it scientifically in the 1960s, this puzzling phenomenon claims hot liquids can sometimes freeze faster than cold ones — what is it called?
Mpemba effect: Natural phenomenon that hot water freezes faster than cold.

Nicknamed the 'flesh-eating disease' even though the bacteria don't actually consume tissue — they release toxins that kill it instead — this fast-spreading infection often enters through a cut or burn. What condition is it?
Necrotizing fasciitis: Infection that results in the death of the body's soft tissue.
Introduced to Hawaii in 1929, this crested songbird serves as the state bird of seven US states including Ohio and Virginia — which bird?
Northern cardinal: Species of North American bird.
Found on every continent but Antarctica, these flowers can lure pollinators by mimicking female insects, and their tiny seeds depend on fungal partners just to sprout. What plant family is this?
Orchid: Family of flowering plants in the order Asparagales.
Secreted by small neck glands when blood calcium runs low, this peptide messenger raises calcium levels and boosts active vitamin D production — which one?
Parathyroid hormone: Mammalian protein found in humans.
This serous membrane lines the abdominal cavity and serves as a conduit for the blood vessels and nerves of the organs it covers — what is it called?
Peritoneum: Membrane that forms lining of abdominal cavity or coelom.

This French polymath's five-volume 'Celestial Mechanics' recast Newtonian physics in the language of calculus, and he pioneered both a widely used integral transform and helped shape Bayesian probability — who is he?
This plant genus — whose members go by names like poplar, aspen, and cottonwood — includes the first tree species ever to have its complete genome sequenced, in 2006 — what genus is it?
Populus: Genus of plants. Populus is a genus of 25–30 species of deciduous flowering plants in the family Salicaceae, native to most of the Northern Hemisphere.
Flagged by the WHO as one of the greatest antibiotic-resistance threats to humans, this rod-shaped bacterium causes hospital infections like ventilator-associated pneumonia — which pathogen?
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Species of bacterium. P. aeruginosa is able to selectively inhibit various antibiotics from penetrating its outer membrane and has high resistance to several antibiotics.
Named for the ragged look of its leaves, this genus of flowering plants causes up to half of all pollen-related allergy cases despite a genus name meaning 'food of the gods' — which plant?
Ragweed: Genus of plants. The name "ragweed" is derived from "ragged" + "weed," coming from the ragged appearance of the plant's leaves.
Native to Europe, northwestern Africa, and southwestern Asia, this flowering shrub's edible fruit stars in desserts and preserves — what's its species name, better known as the gooseberry?
Ribes uva-crispa: Species of flowering plant in the family Grossulariaceae.
Introduced in the 1970s, this database language let programmers grab many records with one single command, eliminating the need to specify an index path to reach each one — what is it?

Originally from the Mediterranean, this yellowish-gray arthropod has up to 15 pairs of long legs and preys on insects with venom too mild to harm humans — what species commonly invades homes worldwide?
Scutigera coleoptrata: Species of arthropod. Scutigera coleoptrata, also known as the house centipede, is a species of centipede that is typically yellowish-gray and has up to 15 pairs of long legs.
Named after a Native American war chief, this four-blade, twin-engine Army helicopter entered service in 1979 to replace the Bell UH-1 Iroquois — which aircraft is it?
Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk: Series of military utility transport helicopters.

Found in Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and northeastern Australia, this large flightless black bird is a close ratite relative of the emu and ostrich, and its Australian population is listed as endangered — which bird?
Southern cassowary: Species of flightless bird. It is one of the three living species of cassowary, alongside the dwarf cassowary and the northern cassowary.
In this eye disorder, the two eyes fail to align properly on the same object, which can cause a lazy eye and lost depth perception if it persists through much of childhood. What condition is it?
Strabismus: Eyes not aligning when looking at something.
Named by Linnaeus in 1753 but called cempōhualxōchitl by the Nahua long before, this genus of Mexican-native flowers is commonly known as marigolds — what's the genus?
This Hungarian-American aerospace pioneer made crucial advances in supersonic and hypersonic airflow, and the agreed boundary of outer space — the "___ line" — bears his name. Who was he?
Theodore von Kármán: Hungarian-American mathematician, aerospace engineer and physicist (1881–1963)
Caused by bacteria producing acid that breaks down enamel, dentin, and cementum, this common condition can turn dental cavities anywhere from yellow to black — what is it?
Tooth decay: Deformation of teeth due to acids produced by bacteria.

This orally contracted disease, caused by Salmonella Typhi bacteria, typically begins six to 30 days after exposure with a gradual high fever, weakness, and abdominal pain. Severe cases may produce distinctive rose-colored skin spots. What is this illness?

Typhoid fever: Disease caused by the bacteria Salmonella Typhi. Typhoid fever, also known as typhoid, is an orally contracted disease caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi bacteria, also called Salmonella Typhi.
This legume, also called the broad bean, can trigger a dangerous reaction called favism in people with a certain metabolic blood disorder — what species is it?
